A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Words in Motion by the same authors. Their main text, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original probing accuracies, representation statistics, control calibration and qualitative steering results on Argoverse 2 Forecasting and Waymo, with additional distribution and correlation analyses in the appendix.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds sparse-autoencoder comparisons, sensitivity analyses, simulated domain-shift forecasting results and inference-latency measurements.

M1.justification: v2 constructs control vectors by applying PCA directly to differences between opposing-feature hidden states. v3 adds an auxiliary sparse autoencoder: differences are pooled in its sparse representation and decoded back into the motion encoder's hidden space before inference. Fully connected, convolutional and MLPMixer variants substantially extend the method.

E1.justification: Argoverse 2 Forecasting and Waymo remain the datasets. v3 adds one synthetic Waymo scenario with future motion slowed by approximately 50% to test zero-shot compensation (Section 5.4). This extends coverage to a specific simulated distribution shift within the existing forecasting task.

E2.justification: The RedMotion, Wayformer and HPTR comparisons are retained. v3 substantially expands comparisons of control-vector construction, explicitly evaluating plain PCA against fully connected SAE, Sparse MLPMixer and ConvSAE configurations (Tables 1–2). The new shifted-Waymo experiment also compares SAE steering against unsteered RedMotion (Table 3).

E3.justification: v3's comparative linearity evaluation targets relative speed changes within ±50%, with method-dependent temperature ranges, whereas v2 reports a single temperature sweep over [-50,50]. New protocols include interpolating the first half of future waypoints to simulate slowdown, SAE configuration sweeps, and an eight-focal-agent latency benchmark. The original transformer training settings are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds explained-variance analyses, control-vector alignment comparisons, SAE-width ablations, encoder-module and speed-threshold sensitivity tests, and a JumpReLU feature-shrinkage analysis (Figures 12–13 and 15; Tables 1–2 and 5–9). It also tests synthetic distribution-shift robustness. The earlier correlation heatmaps and direction-control example are retained, with the latter moved from Appendix A.1 to A.9.

E5.justification: v3 Table 4 newly specifies latency means over 1,000 iterations per configuration. This adds limited repeated-measurement and aggregation information. Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals or significance tests for forecasting and controllability results; embedding standard deviations describe representations rather than experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: Extensive vector-geometry, ablation, forecasting and latency results are added. v2 Figure 5 reports PCA R² of 0.821; v3 Table 2 reports 0.969 under the revised calibration range, so this is not a matched-setting gain. Within v3's comparison, ReLU SAE reaches 0.984. On the new slowed-Waymo scenario, Table 3 reports minADE of 3.271 without steering versus 1.174 for SAE-128 at temperature -50.

T1.justification: v3 adds the standard formula for the already-used CDNV metric in Appendix A.17 and briefly invokes Johnson–Lindenstrauss as motivation for SAE decoding. These additions provide mathematical explanation, but no new proof, formal assumption, derived guarantee or substantive revision of existing mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: v2's central claims concern probing interpretable motion features and using them for inference-time steering. v3 retains these and adds central claims that sparse autoencoding improves control linearity and that calibrated vectors enable zero-shot compensation for unseen dataset characteristics with negligible computational overhead. These additions reshape the abstract, contributions and conclusion.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations linking sparse representations to more distinct control features, interpreting speed/acceleration/agent-vector alignment, and attributing ConvSAE calibration behavior to feature shrinkage (Section 5.3 and Appendix A.16). It also develops the domain-shift interpretation, justifies the ±50% evaluation window, and identifies sensitivity to the low-speed class definition.

D1.justification: v3 documents SAE losses, the reported sparsity weight, Adam optimization, a 10,000-epoch training budget, intermediate dimensions, JumpReLU threshold and patch/kernel settings. Appendix A.11 specifies A6000 hardware, PyTorch Lightning profiling and eager execution for latency measurement. The repository link and original transformer hyperparameters are retained; moving v2 Appendix A.4 into Section 4.4 is not an implementation change.

R1.justification: v3 adds substantial positioning around sparse autoencoders, dictionary learning, JumpReLU and zero-shot generalization. Sections 2.1–2.2 introduce a robotics mechanistic-interpretability novelty claim and distinguish offline SAE use and last-module steering from earlier language-model approaches. The MotionLM citation is removed, and motion-threshold motivation is attributed to the already-cited Waymo dataset paper.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list and conclusion are substantially rewritten around sparse autoencoding and generalization. Existing training details move into the main text, qualitative and quantitative results receive separate subsections, and the appendix is reorganized, including moving title origin to A.1 and the retained qualitative example to A.9.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to show SAE encoding, decoding and control-vector construction. The single calibration display becomes a comparative figure, and v3 adds architecture, explained-variance and shrinkage figures plus nine numbered tables. Existing trajectory examples and distributions are relocated, while speed and acceleration panels are reordered in the probing figures.

improvement.justification: v2 provides probing results, one calibration analysis and selected steering examples, with little testing of control-design choices or failure conditions. v3's direct PCA/SAE comparisons and module, width and threshold ablations substantially strengthen validation and expose failures; documented slowdown and latency experiments make practical claims more assessable. These gains substantially improve empirical support and reproducibility. The broader generalization claims remain supported by only one constructed slowdown scenario, and performance uncertainty is still unreported.
